    Which multivariate method? Ordination and the rest

    Source: vignettes/articles/multivariate-methods.Rmd
    multivariate-methods.Rmd
    library(tidydiversity)

    Multivariate analysis and ordination are not the same thing

    Multivariate analysis is the whole family of methods for data with many response variables measured on the same units: in community ecology, the abundances of all the species at each site. Ordination is one branch of that family. The four branches answer different questions:

    Branch The question Methods tidydiversity
    Ordination What are the main gradients in composition, and where do sites and species lie along them? PCA, CA, DCA, PCoA, NMDS (unconstrained); RDA, CCA, db-RDA (constrained) ord_fit(), autoplot()
    Multivariate tests Does composition differ between groups, or change with a variable? PERMANOVA, test of dispersion, Mantel test, permutation tests of constrained ordinations beta_permanova(), beta_dispersion(), beta_mantel(), ord_test(), ord_effects()
    Classification Which sites form groups, and which species characterise them? Cluster analysis, indicator species stats::hclust() on beta_dist(); beta_indicator()
    Dissimilarity How different is each pair of sites? Bray-Curtis, Jaccard, Sørensen, beta diversity beta_dist(), beta_pair(), beta_multi()

    Ordination is a picture: it reduces many species to a few axes you can plot. A multivariate test is a decision: it gives a p-value. Constrained ordination (RDA, CCA, db-RDA) belongs to both branches: it draws the gradients that your explanatory variables explain, and a permutation test then says whether that explanation is more than chance. Unconstrained ordination (PCA, CA, DCA, PCoA, NMDS) only draws; it tests nothing.

    Choosing: question first, then data, then method

    1. What is the question?

    • Describe the main patterns, with no explanatory variables in mind: unconstrained ordination.
    • Explain composition with measured variables (soil, elevation, treatment): constrained ordination, with ord_test() and ord_effects().
    • Compare groups of sites (treatments, habitats): PERMANOVA (beta_permanova()) with its test of dispersion (beta_dispersion()), or a constrained ordination with the factor.
    • Relate two distance matrices (composition and geography, say): Mantel test (beta_mantel()).
    • Follow treatments over time: principal response curves (ord_prc()).
    • Separate the effects of sets of variables (environment and space): variation partitioning (ord_varpart()).

    2. What are the data? For ordination, the length of the main gradient decides between linear and unimodal methods. ord_advise() measures it as CANOCO does (the longest axis of a detrended correspondence analysis, in standard-deviation units of species turnover):

    Gradient length Use
    below 3 SD linear methods: PCA, RDA (on Hellinger-transformed abundances)
    3 to 4 SD either; both are appropriate
    above 4 SD unimodal methods: CA, CCA

    Distance-based methods (PCoA, NMDS, db-RDA, PERMANOVA) suit any gradient length, with a dissimilarity chosen for the data (Bray-Curtis for abundances, Jaccard or Sørensen for presence-absence).

    3. Let the advisor check. ord_advise() (or tidyvisor()) puts the question and the data together and says which method, which test and which plots, with its reasons:

    d <- community_long(dune_species, cols = -site)
ord_advise(d, abundance = abundance, formula = ~ A1 + Management, env = dune_env)
#> 
#> ── tidyvisor: do the site variables explain composition? ───────────────────────
#> Question: explain
#> 
#> ── What the data show ──
#> 
#> • Sites: 20
#> • Species: 30
#> • Data: abundances
#> • Zeros: 67% — many zeros: shared absences must not make sites similar
#>   (Hellinger or Bray-Curtis)
#> • Species in one site only: 10%
#> • Gradient length (DCA axis 1, SD units): 3.52 — 3 to 4 SD: intermediate;
#>   linear and unimodal methods are both appropriate
#> • Site variables (model terms): 4
#> 
#> ── Recommended ──
#> 
#> Approach: Constrained (direct, canonical) ordination
#> Branch: ordination and multivariate test (a picture with a permutation test).
#> You have a hypothesis that measured site variables explain composition.
#> Method: RDA on Hellinger-transformed data (or db-RDA)
#> Gradient length 3.5 SD.
#> ord <- ord_fit(data, abundance = abundance, method = "rda", transform = "hellinger", formula = ~A1 + Management)
#> Test: Permutation tests: the whole model, each axis and each term
#> The F-test of a constrained ordination has no parametric distribution;
#> permuting sites gives p-values.
#> ord_test(ord, by = "model"); ord_test(ord, by = "axis"); ord_test(ord, by = "margin")
#> Plots: Triplot; species response curves along the main variable; t-value biplot
#> or Van Dobben circles
#> The triplot shows sites, species and variables together; response curves show
#> each species' optimum and tolerance with confidence bands; Van Dobben circles
#> single out the species that respond significantly.
#> autoplot(ord)
#> autoplot(ord, type = "response", variable = "<numeric>")
#> autoplot(ord, type = "vandobben", variable = "<numeric>")
#> Interpret: Plain-language explanation of the tables and the diagram
#> Variation explained, tests, directions of variables, groups, species at each
#> end of the axes, and how to read the plot.
#> ord_interpret(ord)

    The words, briefly

    • Axis (gradient): a combination of species abundances along which sites differ most (unconstrained), or most in relation to the explanatory variables (constrained).
    • Eigenvalue: the variation an axis represents; divided by the total, the share of the variation it shows.
    • Constrained / canonical / direct: the axes are combinations of the explanatory variables. Unconstrained / indirect: the axes come from the species data alone; variables can be fitted afterwards (passively).
    • Partial: the effect of covariables (Condition() in the formula) is removed first.
    • Permutation test: shuffles sites to see how often chance alone gives as strong a result; the shuffling can be restricted for blocked, split-plot, time-series or spatial designs (ord_design()).

    Further reading

    Legendre, P. and Legendre, L. (2012). Numerical Ecology, third edition. Elsevier.

    Leps, J. and Smilauer, P. (2003). Multivariate Analysis of Ecological Data using CANOCO. Cambridge University Press.
